q: Under the usual beam sign convention, when is the shear at a section positive?
o: When the net transverse force on the part left of the cut acts upward
When the net force on the left part acts downward
When the beam sags
When the shear diagram is above the moment diagram
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Positive shear: upward on the left of the cut, downward on the right. A simple beam under gravity load has positive shear near its left support and negative shear near its right support.

q: A beam with fixed ends and a simple beam carry the same uniform load over the same span. How do their midspan deflections compare?
o: They deflect the same
The fixed-ended beam deflects one-fifth as much
The fixed-ended beam deflects twice as much
The fixed-ended beam deflects half as much
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Simple beam: 5wL⁴/384EI. Fixed-ended beam: wL⁴/384EI. End fixity stops the ends rotating, so the beam is five times stiffer at midspan.

q: Which of these is a live load?
o: The weight of the floor slab
The weight of a fixed partition wall
People and movable furniture on a floor
The weight of the roof framing
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Live loads come from use and occupancy and can move or change. The slab, fixed walls and roof framing are permanent, so they are dead loads.

q: What is a distributed load?
o: A load acting at a single point
A load that changes with time
A load from an earthquake
A load spread over a length or an area
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Distributed loads are given per length (kN/m) or per area (kPa). A uniformly distributed load has constant intensity; a varying load, such as soil pressure, does not.

q: What causes a water (ponding) load on a roof?
o: Rainwater collecting because of the roof shape, its deflection or blocked drains
Condensation on the underside of the roof
Water in the concrete mix
Water pipes running across the roof
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: If drains clog, rain builds up; the weight makes the roof sag, and the sag collects more water. Flat roofs must be designed for this and given overflow drains.

q: A 6 m simple beam carries a uniform load of 10 kN/m. What is each support reaction?
o: 60 kN
30 kN
15 kN
20 kN
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: The total load is w × L = 10 × 6 = 60 kN. The load is symmetric, so each support takes half: 30 kN.
steps: Total load W = 10 kN/m × 6 m = 60 kN

q: Under the usual beam sign convention, what does a positive bending moment do?
o: Bends the beam concave downward (hogging), with the top in tension
Twists the beam
Bends the beam concave upward (sagging), with the bottom in tension
Pushes the beam sideways
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Positive moment sags the beam, like a smile: bottom fibres in tension, top in compression. It is found at midspan of simple beams.

q: What makes up occupancy load?
o: The self-weight of the structure
The weight of the roofing
Wind pressure on the walls
People, furniture, stored goods and similar items brought in by the use of a space
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Occupancy load is the live load that comes with the use of a space. NSCP sets minimum values for each use in Table 205-1.

q: A 6 m fixed-ended beam carries a uniform load of 12 kN/m. What is the moment at each fixed end?
o: 36 kN·m
54 kN·m
18 kN·m
72 kN·m
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: For a fixed-ended beam under uniform load, the end moments are wL²/12 = 12 × 36 / 12 = 36 kN·m (negative, hogging). The midspan moment is wL²/24 = 18 kN·m.

q: In structural terms, what is a load?
o: Only the weight of people
Any force or action that a structure must resist
Only the weight of the structure
Only the force of wind
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Loads include weights (dead and live), environmental actions (wind, earthquake, rain) and imposed effects such as settlement and temperature change.

q: What effect does uneven (differential) settlement of foundations have on a structure?
o: None, as long as the soil is dry
It only affects the finishes
It imposes extra forces and moments, like a load
It reduces the dead load
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: When one support sinks more than another, a continuous or fixed structure is forced to bend, which creates stresses and cracks. NSCP counts restrained differential movement among the loads.

q: A 3 m cantilever carries a 10 kN point load at its free end. What is the moment at the fixed end?
o: 10 kN·m
15 kN·m
45 kN·m
30 kN·m
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: M = P × L = 10 kN × 3 m = 30 kN·m, hogging (tension at the top). That is why a cantilever's main bars go at the top.
steps: P = 10 kN at the free end

q: Which of these is a dead load?
o: A permanently fixed water heater
Occupants
Movable office furniture
Stored boxes
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Dead load includes the structure and everything permanently fixed to it, such as fixed service equipment. Items that can be moved or removed are live load.

q: A 5 m simple beam carries a 20 kN point load 2 m from the left support. What is the left reaction?
o: 8 kN
12 kN
10 kN
20 kN
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Take moments about the right support: RL × 5 = 20 × 3, so RL = 12 kN. The right reaction is 20 − 12 = 8 kN. The support nearer the load takes more.
steps: Distance from load to right support b = 5 − 2 = 3 m

q: A balcony slab projects from a building and is held down by the floor slab behind it. What kind of member is the balcony?
o: A simple beam
A continuous beam
A cantilever
A suspended span
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: A cantilever projects past its support and relies on fixity or a back-span to stay in balance. Its top bars must extend well back into the floor slab.

q: What curvature goes with a negative (hogging) bending moment?
o: Concave upward, with the bottom in tension
No curvature at all
A twist about the axis
Concave downward (convex), with the top in tension
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Negative moment is found over interior supports of continuous beams and at cantilever roots. The top fibres are in tension there, so the main bars go at the top.

q: What is a static load?
o: A load applied slowly, with no rapid change in size or position
A load that causes vibration
A sudden impact load
A moving crane load
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Static loads build up gradually, so the structure has time to respond without dynamic effects. Impact, vibrating machinery and earthquakes are dynamic.

q: What is a concentrated load?
o: A load spread evenly along a beam
A load acting on a very small area, idealized as a point
A load spread over a whole floor
A load that changes over time
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: A column bearing on a girder or a wheel on a slab is treated as a point load, expressed in kN.

q: What is a double overhanging beam?
o: A beam fixed at both ends
A beam on three supports
A beam on two supports that extends past both of them
A cantilever with a prop
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Overhangs at both ends reduce the positive span moment and create negative moment over both supports. The beam is still statically determinate.

q: What makes a beam a simple beam?
o: It is fixed at both ends
It spans over more than two supports
It is supported at one end only
It rests on supports at both ends that let it rotate and do not resist moment
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: A simple beam sits on a pin and a roller. There is no moment at the supports, and its reactions come from equilibrium alone.

q: What is an overhanging beam?
o: A simple beam that extends past one of its supports
A beam fixed at one end and free at the other
A beam fixed at both ends
A beam supported at midspan only
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Extending past a support creates negative moment over it and reduces the positive moment in the span.

q: Is a point of inflection in a continuous beam a physical hinge?
o: Yes; the beam is pinned there
No; it is only where the moment happens to be zero, and the beam stays continuous there
Yes; it is a construction joint
No; it is where the shear is greatest
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: At an inflection point the curvature changes sign and the moment is zero, but the beam still carries shear and remains continuous. A real hinge exists only where one is built in.

q: Under the usual beam sign convention, when is the shear at a section negative?
o: When the net force on the left part acts upward
When the beam hogs
When the net transverse force on the part left of the cut acts downward
When the moment is zero
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: Negative shear: downward on the left of the cut. In a simple beam under uniform load, shear is positive near the left support, zero at midspan and negative near the right.

q: What happens to the curvature of a beam at a point of inflection?
o: It is at its greatest value
It becomes infinite
It doubles
It changes sign, from sagging to hogging or the reverse
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Ch. 2
n: At the point of inflection the curvature and the moment are both zero. Bar cut-offs and splices are often placed with reference to these points.
